explanations.explanation: The priests, yes! The LORD says, “Ask the priests for a ruling.” Haggai, the prophet getting this word, doesn't offer his own opinion. He takes the question straight to the people the LORD named.

Good guess, but the elders aren't who the LORD names here. He says, “Ask the priests for a ruling.” Haggai, the prophet receiving this word, takes the question to them. The elders just didn't get a ticket for this one.
I see why you'd think a ruling goes to the judges, but the LORD names someone else. He says, “Ask the priests for a ruling.” So Haggai, the prophet, puts his question to the priests. No gavel needed.

Close, but the text says the opposite. The priests answer, “No,” replied the priests, and that's the ruling. The meat is consecrated, yet the food it touches does not become holy. Holiness doesn't spread just by touching.

Right, it's false. The question is whether the food becomes holy, and “No,” replied the priests. The consecrated meat can touch bread, stew, wine, oil or any other food, and none of it becomes holy. One word, and it settles it.

Defiled is the word. Haggai asks about someone defiled by contact with a corpse, and the priests answer, “Yes, it becomes defiled.” Notice the shift from the first question. A flat no turns into a clear yes. This one is a heavy subject, so I'll just say plainly that the ruling is clear.

Holy was the answer to the first question, and even there the priests said no. Here Haggai asks about someone defiled by contact with a corpse. The priests answer, “Yes, it becomes defiled.” So the food ends up defiled, not holy.

Clean sounds nice, but it's not what the priests say. Haggai asks about someone defiled by contact with a corpse touching any of these foods. They answer, “Yes, it becomes defiled.” It's a serious subject, and the ruling goes the other way.

True. Haggai says, “…and so it is with every work of their hands; whatever they offer there is defiled.” The priests' rulings were about food, and now Haggai applies them to the people and the nation. This is a hard word, and the LORD declares it plainly.

Not this time, baker. After the two rulings, Haggai says for the LORD, “…and so it is with every work of their hands; whatever they offer there is defiled.” So the answer is true. It's a hard line to hear, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: Before one stone sat on another
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “Now consider carefully from this day forward: Before one stone was placed on another in the temple of the LORD…” He points them back to the time before any building had started. Then He tells them what they saw in those days.

explanations.answer: Before its gold was carried off
explanations.explanation: Gold isn't mentioned in this passage. The LORD points them back to a time “Before one stone was placed on another in the temple of the LORD.” That's the starting line He wants them to remember. I'd love to say more about gold, but the verse doesn't.
Doors never come up here. The LORD says, “Before one stone was placed on another in the temple of the LORD.” So the time He means is before the building started. Nothing about shutting anything.
Not quite. Someone came expecting a heap of twenty ephahs of grain and found only ten. That's half of what they hoped for. It's the kind of surprise that makes you check the bag twice.

False is right. Someone came expecting a heap of twenty ephahs of grain and found only ten. The winepress told the same story, fifty baths expected and only twenty drawn out. Half a heap or less, and nobody likes that math.

explanations.answer: They did not turn to Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the line. The LORD says, “…but you did not turn to Me, declares the LORD.” He had struck all the work of their hands with blight, mildew and hail. And through all of that, the text says they did not turn to Him.

That's the opposite of what the LORD says. After the blight, mildew and hail, He says, “…but you did not turn to Me, declares the LORD.” The text doesn't say they cried out. It says they did not turn to Him.

The text never says they left their fields. It says the LORD struck all the work of their hands, “…but you did not turn to Me, declares the LORD.” That's what He says the people did. I think it's worth holding onto that line.

explanations.answer: The foundation of the LORD's temple was laid
explanations.explanation: Yes! The LORD names the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month as “…the day the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid…” That's the very day He is speaking to them. The foundation is down, and He tells them to consider carefully from this day on.

explanations.answer: The LORD's temple was finished at last
explanations.explanation: The text says something earlier in the building. The twenty-fourth day of the ninth month is “…the day the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid…” A foundation is the first layer, not the finish line. So the work is just getting underway.

explanations.answer: The ark was brought into the temple
explanations.explanation: The ark isn't mentioned in this passage. The LORD says that day is “…the day the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid…” That's the event He wants them to remember. It's a day for a foundation.

Not yet, and that's exactly what the verse says. “The vine, the fig, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not yet yielded fruit.” The LORD points to empty branches and an empty barn before He gives His promise. So the honest answer is false.
False, you got it. “The vine, the fig, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not yet yielded fruit.” Nothing is on the branches yet. And then the LORD turns it around with a promise.

Bless is the word, and what a way to end. The LORD says, “But from this day on, I will bless you.” The barn question and the bare trees come first, and then comes that promise. I think it's a good one to read twice.
Test isn't the word. The LORD says, “But from this day on, I will bless you.” The promise is a blessing. After all those hard lines, I think that's a warm place to land.
Scatter isn't what He says. He says, “But from this day on, I will bless you.” It's a promise of blessing, plain and simple. And it begins from this day on.
